1:
The psalm opens without a subject, and the roster accounts for that in four ways. Adam Clarke suspects damage: it begins and ends so abruptly that many have thought it only a fragment of a larger psalm, an opinion he calls very likely. Charles Ellicott denies that anything is missing. The verbless clause has led to a conjecture that a line has dropped away, but this is unnecessary if we neglect the accents and take the gates of Zion in apposition with his foundation: his foundation on the holy hill loveth Jehovah, even Zion’s gates, more than all Jacob’s dwellings. John Gill and Matthew Henry report the older solution, that the Jewish writers and the Targum join the first words to the title, so that the psalm announces the holy mountains as its subject. C.H. Spurgeon needs no explanation but temperament: the poet’s heart was full and gained vent on a sudden, and though sudden passion is evil, bursts of holy joy are precious.

What is founded there is then described very differently. Matthew Henry works the figure hard: the church has a foundation and cannot sink or totter, being built high on the top of the mountains and firmly, since the mountains are rocky — whereas the world is founded upon the seas, continually ebbing and flowing, and Babel was built in a plain where the ground was rotten. C.H. Spurgeon makes the founding an act of election: God might have selected other spots, and his choice made the mountains holy; the church is founded not on the sand of carnal policy nor in the morass of human kingdoms but in the eternal and invincible decrees. Rome stands on her seven hills, he adds, and has never lacked a poet’s tongue to sing her glories, but more glorious far art thou, O Zion. Adam Clarke keeps to the survey: Jerusalem was founded on Zion and Moriah, and the later increase of population obliged the inhabitants to enclose the contiguous hills. Charles Ellicott thinks the plural only poetical, though geographically correct, citing Dean Stanley on the multiplicity of eminences the city shares with Rome and Constantinople.

Which city is meant is the real division. John Gill allows that the literal Jerusalem was magnificent and had glorious things said of it, the Messiah coming into it and suffering near it, but takes the verse of the church. Adam Clarke makes the same move about the gates: mystically the Lord prefers the Christian Church to the Jewish, the latter being only a type, and to this position, he says, no exception can be made. Augustine of Hippo takes the city as one we have not reached: its citizens are we, as far as we are Christians, absent while we are mortal and tending towards it, so that what is sung is the song of a longing heart — he who truly longs singing within his soul though his tongue be silent, while he who does not, however he may resound in human ears, is voiceless to God. Keil and Delitzsch read it as prophecy about the nations, in a style concise even to obscurity, which Eusebius called exceedingly enigmatic and darkly expressed; and since Rahab and Babylon stand first among the peoples brought in, they date it after the destruction of the Assyrian army before Jerusalem. John Calvin gives the practical use: the children of this world extol their own condition and look on the Church with contempt while God keeps her low and despised; the sum of the psalm is that she far excels all the kingdoms and politics of the world, being watched over and protected by him. John Wesley notes that Zion is named rather than Jerusalem to intimate that God loved the city for the temple’s sake, and Charles Ellicott that the praise of Zion had already found many tongues, the poet meaning to swell the chorus.
4:
Rahab is agreed to be Egypt; the reasons given for the name vary. John Gill rules out the harlot of that name, since the letters of the two words are not the same in Hebrew, and offers a choice: the country may be so called from the pride of its inhabitants, whom Philo the Jew describes as naturally proud, or from a city of the name, or rather from the part called Delta, whose pear-like shape gave it the Egyptian word for pear — whence Athribis, the heart of a pear. Charles Ellicott says the origin of the term is much disputed and thinks it most probably a word, possibly Coptic, for a large sea or river monster symbolic of Egypt.

What the clause about being born there means divides the entry, and Charles Ellicott says the whole intention of the psalm turns on it. Immediately after the mention of a place, he argues, there must refer to that place and not to one named in the previous verse; the poet is enumerating renowned nations much as Horace does, only instead of leaving them as a theme to others he tells us what he himself might say of them and of how their natives were esteemed. From this he draws a conclusion he says it is hardly possible to escape: the Palestinian Jew is implying his superiority to those of his own race born abroad, the same spirit that appears in the relations of the Hebrews to the Hellenistic Jews. Matthew Henry reads it as a concession followed by a promise. Other places have their glories, and here and there one famous man eminent for knowledge and virtue was a native of them; but some give another sense, that this is a prophecy of bringing the Gentiles in, God owning them as born in Zion and born again there, so that a Gentile convert stands level with a native Jew. John Wesley takes the same line, understanding by Egypt and Philistia all the enemies of the church, now not only reconciled but united to it, and allowing that the name Rahab may come from pride or from natural strength. Adam Clarke hears only comparison: to be born in any of these is no privilege beside being a native of Jerusalem, since their cities are but heads of villages while Jerusalem alone is a City. He adds a parallel from a Persian work whose author he does not know, asking what celebrity Egypt or Syria can pretend to beside one city.

The next verse answers that comparison. Charles Ellicott takes it as antithetical to the preceding, the poet claiming a prouder boast for natives of Jerusalem because the Most High established her. John Wesley reads the doubled word as man and man, all sorts of men without difference of nations, and finds in the establishing a promise of no transient but a lasting work. Adam Clarke allows the honour and then raises it: how much greater to be born from above and be a citizen of the Jerusalem which is above. He notes too the Targum’s gloss that David and Solomon were brought up here.

The writing up of the people is either civic or divine. Charles Ellicott takes it for the census or birth-register of citizens, lists he thinks were produced in triumph to mark a native of Jerusalem off from those born at a distance, and John Wesley makes the same allusion to princes who keep a register of their people. John Gill makes it divine but careful: not the Lamb’s book of life, written from eternity, but the enrolment among the living in Jerusalem at effectual calling, or the numbering of God’s people at the last day. Adam Clarke agrees: when God takes account of all professing Christians he will set apart as inhabitants of the New Jerusalem those born in Zion, that is, born again.
7:
Everyone finds the last verse hard. Charles Ellicott calls it this most obscure verse and gives its literal sense as and singers as trumpeters, all my springs in Thee, which he paraphrases in line with the rest of the psalm: for such an one, celebrating his birthday, the singers and musicians will sing to Zion, all my offspring is in Thee. Not only is it a boast to have been born there; in the genuine Hebrew spirit the boast is carried on into future generations, and the Hebrew of the Hebrews exults in addressing the sacred city as the cradle of his family. The figurative use of springs for posterity, he adds, is well attested elsewhere.

Adam Clarke says outright that the whole psalm is obscure and difficult, and then does something he does nowhere else here: instead of notes he ventures a literal version of the entire psalm with a few explanatory interpolations, to cast a little more light upon it. Along the way he records the textual state. Many manuscripts and early printed editions read princes rather than singers; some would read habitations for my fountains, with several of the versions, but no manuscript yet discovered supports that reading. He takes the fountains for ancestors and posterity, noting that springs, wells, cisterns and waters are used metaphorically in the sacred writings for children, posterity and people, and finds the exultation natural enough — it would be a great thing to know that all one’s friends, family and children were citizens of this royal city, entered in God’s register and entitled to his protection. Applied to the Christian Church, he says, the privileges are higher still. For the rendering itself he follows a version he thinks decisive, since Symmachus and another ancient Greek translator, who must have known the sense of the Hebrew text well, made the line run that they shall sing, as in leading up a dance, all my fountains are in thee. He observes as well that the old Psalter understands the whole psalm as relating to Gospel times, and that Bishop Horne takes it in the same sense.

What is being sung, and by whom, is read more simply by the others. John Gill puts the singers and players in Zion, that is in the church, taking the verse to signify the great spiritual joy there when these things are accomplished — joy in the churches at the conversion of Jews and Gentiles, and joy in the persons themselves, born again and brought to Zion — the whole in allusion to the vocal and instrumental music used in the temple service. John Wesley says the same and states the principle behind it: the psalmist describes evangelical worship by legal phrases and customs, as the prophets frequently do. He also takes the closing words as the burden of the song, sung in the name of all the people of God: all our desires and delights are in thee, and all the springs of mercy, grace and glory flow to us only in and through thee.
